Mental Health Care Plan

Patient & GP Details
- Patient: John Doe, DOB: 17/11/1991, Gender: Not recorded, Contact: Not recorded, Address: Not recorded
- Referring GP: Dr Deen Mirza, Practice: Babylon, Practice Address: Not recorded. Provider No.: Not recorded, Contact: Not recorded

Clinical Assessment

Identified Problems/Provisional Diagnoses:
- Principal: Large local allergic reaction to insect sting (localized urticaria/inflammatory reaction) — High likelihood
- Secondary: Early/evolving IgE-mediated anaphylaxis / systemic allergic reaction — Medium likelihood
- Tertiary: Anxiety / panic-related dyspnea (acute health anxiety reaction) — Medium likelihood

Clinical Details & History:
- Medications: None reported. (No regular medications documented.)
- Allergies/ADRs: Penicillin allergy reported.
- Past Medical History: Eczema.

Mental Health History:
- Previous Diagnoses: Not recorded (patient reports occasional anxiety/panic attacks but no formal diagnosis documented).
- Past Treatments (Therapy, Medications, Hospitalizations): No prior medication for anxiety reported; no hospitalisations for allergy/anaphylaxis recorded.
- Family History: No family history of acute allergic reactions recorded. (No mental health family history recorded.)

Social & Lifestyle Factors:
- Living Situation: Lives alone.
- Social Support: Not recorded.
- Occupation/Education: Works as a computer scientist.
- Alcohol Use: Not recorded.
- Smoking/Substance Use: Not recorded.
- Key Stressors: Acute anxiety about potential progression to anaphylaxis following recent insect sting.

Mental Status Examination (MSE):
- Appearance & General Behaviour: Cooperative, communicative; speaking normally during remote consultation; no obvious respiratory distress observed by clinician.
- Mood & Affect: Anxious (patient reports feeling anxious about breathing and potential worsening).
- Speech & Thought: Speech fluent and coherent; thought process not disorganized.
- Perception: No hallucinations or perceptual disturbances reported.

Cognition:
- Orientation: Not recorded.
- Attention/Concentration: Not recorded.
- Memory: Not recorded.
- Insight & Judgement: Appears to understand risk and appropriate actions (sought medical advice promptly and followed clinician instructions).

Physical Symptoms:
- Sleep: Not recorded.
- Appetite: Not recorded.
- Motivation/Energy: Not recorded.
- Anxiety Symptoms: Reports subjective breathlessness, sensation of lip/tongue oddness, and worry about progression; history of occasional anxiety/panic.

Risk Assessment:
- Suicidal/Self-Harm/Risk to Others: No suicidal ideation or self-harm intent reported. No risk to others identified.
- Protective Factors: Help-seeking behaviour (contacted clinician promptly); currently speaking normally and ambulatory; clinician assessment finds no objective airway compromise.
- Overall Current Risk Level (Self): Low for self-harm. (No suicidal ideation reported; immediate medical risk judged low by clinician for airway compromise at time of assessment.)
- Emergency Contact: Not recorded.

Formulation:
- Predisposing factors: History of eczema and prior allergic diathesis; occasional baseline anxiety.
- Precipitating factors: Recent insect sting (bee/wasp) minutes prior to presentation triggered local inflammatory response and health anxiety.
- Perpetuating factors: Anxiety about potential anaphylaxis amplifying perception of breathlessness and oral sensations; lack of immediate antihistamine use.
- Protective factors: No objective airway compromise on remote exam, patient able to communicate and seek care, clinician provided immediate advice and education.
- Integrative formulation: The presentation is most consistent with a large local allergic reaction causing localized erythema and discomfort. Subjective dyspnea and oral sensations are likely a combination of mild systemic histamine-mediated effects and anxiety amplification. Early anaphylaxis is a differential due to rapid onset after sting and reported symptoms; clinician assessment and remote exam did not demonstrate objective airway compromise or systemic instability at the time of consultation. Patient education and monitoring are appropriate; escalate to emergency care if signs of systemic reaction develop.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem:
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Reduce acute anxiety about breathing and prevent escalation of symptoms.
  - Achieve symptom control of local reaction.
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Control allergic/inflammatory response at sting site.
  - Rapid identification and management if systemic allergic reaction/anaphylaxis develops.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Take an oral antihistamine (over-the-counter options discussed). Example given: chlorphenamine (Piriton) 4 mg tablet — up to every 4–6 hours as needed (clinician advised: one tablet, 4 mg, up to six times/day). Alternatively a once-daily non-sedating antihistamine may be used. (Dose/route/frequency documented as advised by clinician; patient to follow product instructions or pharmacist advice.)
  - Monitor sting site and general symptoms closely (watch for spreading redness, increasing warmth, new/worsening swelling, breathing difficulty, dizziness, or collapse).
  - If symptoms worsen or systemic signs develop, go to Emergency Department immediately or call emergency services.
  - Contact clinician promptly if concerned or if symptoms progress.
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Provide patient education materials (clinician to leave link about anaphylactic reactions).
  - Advise over-the-counter antihistamine use as above.
  - Advise monitoring for local infection (if redness spreads/warmth develops consider review for possible need for antibiotics).
  - Arrange urgent assessment or direct patient to A&E if any signs of airway compromise or systemic deterioration.

Secondary Problem:
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Recognize signs of anaphylaxis and seek immediate emergency care.
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Prevent progression to life-threatening anaphylaxis; ensure timely emergency response if it occurs.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Attend Emergency Department immediately if new/worsening difficulty breathing, stridor, progressive lip/tongue swelling, generalized urticaria, dizziness, fainting, or collapse.
  - Do not wait for scheduled appointment if rapid progression is suspected.
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Clearly advise criteria for emergency presentation (documented in education materials).
  - Consider further evaluation if recurrent similar reactions occur (e.g., allergy referral/testing) — not indicated at this single localized event per clinician but to be considered if recurrent.

Tertiary Problem (Anxiety / Panic-related dyspnea):
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Reduce acute anxiety and learn immediate coping strategies for breathlessness/anxiety.
  - Prevent future distressing panic responses related to medical events.
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Reduce acute anxiety symptoms and reduce healthcare avoidance or excessive health-related anxiety.
  - Offer referral to mental health support if anxiety becomes recurrent or impairing.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Use calming strategies (slow controlled breathing, grounding techniques) during acute anxiety episodes.
  - Contact clinician for reassurance if anxious; seek urgent care if physical signs suggest systemic reaction.
  - Seek follow-up for anxiety management if episodes are frequent or impairing.
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Provide brief reassurance and education about difference between subjective breathlessness from anxiety vs objective respiratory compromise; supply information link as documented.
  - Offer follow-up contact to discuss anxiety if needed; consider referral to mental health services (e.g., counseling/CBT) if anxiety/panic episodes become frequent — to be discussed if/when patient requests or if symptoms persist.

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention:
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered: recognition of anaphylaxis signs (lip/tongue swelling, breathing difficulty, stridor, dizziness/collapse), over-the-counter antihistamine use, when to seek A&E, monitoring for local infection.
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening:
  - New or progressive lip/tongue swelling, difficulty breathing, noisy inspiratory breath sounds (stridor), generalized urticaria, lightheadedness, fainting, rapidly spreading redness or increasing warmth at sting site.
- Coping Strategies:
  - Use oral antihistamine as advised; practice slow controlled breathing; seek clinician contact for reassurance; attend A&E promptly for any systemic signs.

Consent, Coordination & Review:
- Patient Consent to Plan: Yes (patient verbal agreement and participation in plan documented).
- Copy of Mental Health Care Plan Given to Patient: Not recorded.
- Other Mental Health Professionals Involved in Patient Care: Not recorded.
- GP Acknowledgment (if completed by other MH Professional): Not recorded.
- Review Date: Not recorded (patient advised to re-contact/prioritize A&E if deterioration; follow-up as needed).

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Large local allergic reaction (localized urticaria/inflammatory reaction) — High likelihood.
  - Justification: Puncture mark and localized redness/blotchy rash at sting site with no objective airway compromise; clinician and DDx identify this as most likely.
- Early/evolving IgE-mediated anaphylaxis (systemic allergic reaction) — Medium likelihood.
  - Justification: Temporal onset minutes after sting and patient-reported breathlessness and oral sensations raise concern; absence of objective respiratory compromise or hypotension at assessment lowers immediate likelihood but requires monitoring.
- Anxiety / panic-related dyspnea — Medium likelihood.
  - Justification: Patient reports occasional anxiety and is understandably anxious about potential worsening; clinician observed normal speech and breathing suggesting subjective amplification of symptoms.

Quality checks
● Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Vital signs (respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, heart rate, blood pressure) not recorded.
  - Formal mental health diagnostic history and psychiatric medication history not recorded.
  - Emergency contact details and explicit documented review/follow-up appointment date not recorded.
  - Copy of care plan provision to patient not documented.
● Internal conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - None significant; transcript clinician concluded localized reaction and DDx ranks local reaction as highest likelihood while retaining early anaphylaxis and anxiety as relevant differentials — consistent.
● Transcript quality notes:
  - Transcript appears complete and clear; remote visual inspection of oropharynx and arm site documented; no audio quality issues recorded.
